questions.stem: In VCE Politics, legitimacy is best described as:
options: the belief that a ruler or institution has the right to exercise power
the ability of an actor to force others to act against their own will
the number of seats a party wins in parliament at a general election
the set of written rules that describes how a state's government works
questions.explanation: Legitimacy is the belief, held by those who are governed, that a ruler or institution has the right to exercise power. The ability to force others to act is coercive power, which can exist without any legitimacy at all.

questions.stem: According to the study of politics, legitimacy transforms power into:
options: authority
coercion
ideology
federalism
questions.explanation: When people accept that an actor has the right to exercise power, that power becomes authority. Coercion is the use of force or threats, which is what an actor falls back on when it lacks legitimacy.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates 'power over' others, as distinct from 'power to' do something?
options: A ruler orders security forces to detain critics without charge to silence opposition
A local council uses its own budget to build a new public library that its residents asked for
A parliament passes a law setting up a new national scheme for disability support
A charity uses its donations to run a literacy program in remote communities
questions.explanation: 'Power over' is the coercive use of power to control other actors or ordinary people, as in detaining critics to silence them. Building a library, passing a law to create a scheme or running a program are examples of 'power to', the capacity to achieve something.

questions.stem: A regime stays in power by imprisoning opponents and using surveillance to deter protest. Which judgement about the regime is most accurate?
options: It has strong democratic legitimacy, because few of its citizens openly oppose the government
It rests on popular sovereignty, because its citizens have chosen not to take part in protests
It has legitimacy based on economic performance, because its security forces are well funded
It relies on coercion, which can produce compliance but not genuine belief in its right to rule
questions.explanation: Coercion can keep a regime in power by making people comply out of fear, but compliance is not the same as believing the regime has a right to rule. A lack of open opposition under surveillance and imprisonment is not evidence of democratic legitimacy, because people are not free to oppose.

questions.stem: Popular sovereignty is the principle that:
options: a state has supreme authority within its own borders, free from interference by other states
the Crown is the source of all executive power, which ministers exercise on its behalf
ultimate political authority rests with the people, who express it through elections and referendums
parliament may make or unmake any law on any subject, and no other body can override its laws
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty places ultimate authority with the people, who exercise it by electing representatives and, in Australia, by voting in referendums to change the Constitution. The principle that parliament can make or unmake any law is parliamentary sovereignty.

questions.stem: Why is parliamentary sovereignty more limited in Australia than in the United Kingdom?
options: Australian voters can overturn any Act of parliament by presenting a petition with enough signatures
Australian parliaments may pass only those laws that the Governor-General has first recommended
Australian parliaments must act within a written Constitution that the High Court can enforce
Australian Acts must be approved by the monarch's ministers in London before they take effect
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Parliament can make laws only within the powers the Constitution gives it, and the High Court can declare a law invalid if it goes beyond them. The United Kingdom has no single written constitution of this kind. Australian laws do not need approval from British ministers.

questions.stem: Political participation refers to:
options: the right of the High Court to decide whether a law is within the Constitution
the convention that ministers must be members of the parliament they answer to
the ways citizens take part in political life, such as voting, joining parties and protesting
the division of law-making powers between the Commonwealth and the six states under the Constitution
questions.explanation: Participation covers the many ways citizens take part in politics, from voting to joining a party, campaigning, making submissions or protesting. The division of law-making powers is federalism, and the requirement that ministers sit in parliament is part of responsible government.

questions.stem: Federalism is a system of government in which:
options: the people vote directly on every major law proposed by the government of the day
power is divided between a central government and regional governments, each with its own powers
all power is held by one national government, which may delegate some tasks to local councils
the executive is drawn from the parliament and must keep the confidence of the lower house
questions.explanation: In a federation such as Australia, the Constitution divides power between the Commonwealth and the states, so each level has its own areas of authority. A system in which one national government holds all power and may delegate it is a unitary system.

questions.stem: In a unitary state, unlike a federation:
options: regional governments have powers guaranteed by the Constitution that cannot be removed
the central government cannot pass laws on any matter given to regional governments
a referendum is needed whenever the central government wishes to make a new law
regional governments have only the powers the central government chooses to give them
questions.explanation: In a unitary state, sovereignty rests with the central government, so any regional or local bodies hold only the powers it delegates and can have them taken away. Constitutionally guaranteed regional powers are the defining feature of a federation such as Australia.

questions.stem: A valid Commonwealth law and a Victorian law are inconsistent with each other. Under the Constitution:
options: both laws are invalid until the two parliaments agree on a single compromise law
the law passed most recently prevails, whichever parliament made it
the Commonwealth law prevails, and the state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency
the Victorian law prevails, because the states held their powers before Federation
questions.explanation: Section 109 of the Constitution provides that where a state law is inconsistent with a valid Commonwealth law, the Commonwealth law prevails and the state law is invalid to the extent of the inconsistency. The date each law was passed does not decide the matter.

questions.stem: A state government refuses to adopt a Commonwealth policy in an area that the Constitution leaves to the states. What does this best illustrate?
options: Parliamentary sovereignty lets each state parliament override valid Commonwealth laws
The separation of powers makes the state governments part of the federal judiciary
Federalism disperses power, so the states can act as a check on the Commonwealth
Responsible government lets a state parliament dismiss the Commonwealth ministry
questions.explanation: Because the Constitution gives the states their own areas of power, a state can refuse to follow the Commonwealth in those areas, which limits the concentration of power in Canberra. A state cannot override a valid Commonwealth law, because section 109 makes the Commonwealth law prevail.

questions.stem: Which feature is central to responsible government in Australia?
options: Judges are appointed by the governing party and are answerable to it through parliament
Each minister is chosen by voters at a separate election held for that ministry
Ministers are members of parliament, and the government must keep the confidence of the lower house
The head of the executive is elected separately from parliament by a direct national vote
questions.explanation: Under responsible government the executive is drawn from parliament and is answerable to it, and a government holds office only while it has the confidence of the House of Representatives. A head of the executive elected separately from parliament is a feature of presidential systems such as the United States.

questions.stem: By convention, an Australian government must resign or advise an election if it:
options: has one of its laws declared invalid by the High Court
falls behind the opposition in national opinion polls
loses the confidence of the House of Representatives
loses a vote on any of its bills in the Senate
questions.explanation: Responsible government means a government survives only while it has the confidence of the lower house, where it is formed. Losing a vote on a bill in the Senate is common and does not by itself require the government to resign.

questions.stem: A minister is found to have misled parliament about serious failures in their own department, and resigns. Which principle does this best illustrate?
options: The separation of judicial power
The division of powers between the Commonwealth and states
Individual ministerial responsibility
Collective cabinet responsibility
questions.explanation: Individual ministerial responsibility holds each minister accountable to parliament for their own conduct and their department, and misleading parliament is traditionally a resigning matter. Collective cabinet responsibility is about ministers publicly supporting all cabinet decisions.

questions.stem: A minister privately argued against a cabinet decision but defends it in public once it is made. Which convention does this reflect?
options: Parliamentary sovereignty
Popular sovereignty
Collective cabinet responsibility
Individual ministerial responsibility
questions.explanation: Collective cabinet responsibility requires all ministers to support cabinet decisions publicly, whatever their private views, so the government presents a united front to parliament. Individual ministerial responsibility concerns a minister's accountability for their own conduct and department.

questions.stem: In Australia, the separation of powers is strictest between:
options: the Senate and the House of Representatives
the Commonwealth and the state governments
the judiciary and the other two arms of government
the legislature and the executive arms of government
questions.explanation: The Constitution keeps Commonwealth judicial power separate from the legislature and the executive, and the High Court has enforced that separation strictly. The legislature and the executive overlap under responsible government, because ministers sit in parliament.

questions.stem: How does the United States system differ from Australia's in the way it organises executive power?
options: The President is elected separately and does not sit in Congress
The President must be a serving member of the United States Senate
The President is chosen by the Supreme Court from members of Congress
The President is appointed by the state governors after each election
questions.explanation: The United States has a presidential system with a stronger separation of executive and legislative power: the President is elected separately and is not a member of Congress. In Australia the Prime Minister and ministers must be members of parliament.

questions.stem: A government claims the right to rule because it won a free and fair election. Its legitimacy is based on:
options: ideology
democratic processes
economic performance
coercion
questions.explanation: Winning a free and fair election is a democratic source of legitimacy, because the people have consented to the government through voting. Coercion relies on force and fear rather than consent.

questions.stem: A one-party state holds no competitive elections but points to decades of rising incomes as proof of its right to govern. Its main claimed source of legitimacy is:
options: economic performance
democratic processes
popular sovereignty through referendums
the separation of powers
questions.explanation: The government justifies its rule by its record of delivering prosperity, which is legitimacy based on economic performance. It cannot claim democratic legitimacy, because it holds no competitive elections.

questions.stem: A ruling party says its right to govern comes from leading the nation's revolution and building society according to its official doctrine. This narrative relies mainly on:
options: democratic processes
ideology
coercion
economic performance
questions.explanation: The party grounds its claim in a set of ideas, its official doctrine and its revolutionary mission, which is legitimacy based on ideology. Coercion would mean relying on force rather than on a justifying set of beliefs.

questions.stem: A government whose legitimacy rests mainly on regular competitive elections is most likely to:
options: rely on the armed forces to enforce policies that are unpopular
bypass parliament, because winning makes all its decisions valid
respond to public opinion, because it must face the voters again
ignore public opinion, because its term in office is guaranteed
questions.explanation: Where legitimacy comes from elections, a government that loses public support can lose office, so it has a strong reason to respond to public opinion. The source of legitimacy shapes how power is exercised: a government relying on coercion has less need to listen.

questions.stem: During a dispute over a new freeway, a premier says: 'We took this project to the election and won. We have a mandate to build it.' This is best described as:
options: a legitimising narrative based on democratic processes
a legitimising narrative based on economic performance
a claim of authority based on the separation of powers
a claim of legitimacy based on coercion of the voters
questions.explanation: Claiming a mandate from an election win is a legitimising narrative grounded in democratic process: the premier says the voters consented to the project. An argument from economic performance would point to the jobs or growth the project brings rather than to the election result.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-government organisation?
options: The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
Amnesty International
The High Court of Australia
The Australian Electoral Commission
questions.explanation: Amnesty International is a non-government organisation: it is independent of governments and campaigns on human rights. The High Court, the Australian Electoral Commission and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade are all part of the Commonwealth's formal institutions.

questions.stem: In a dispute over a proposed mine, which actor is a formal political institution?
options: The mining company seeking approval to dig the mine
A local residents' action group campaigning against the mine
A national environmental group that opposes the mine
A state parliamentary committee inquiring into the mine
questions.explanation: A parliamentary committee is part of the legislature, one of the formal institutions of government. The company, the residents' group and the environmental group are all actors outside the formal institutions who try to influence the decision.

questions.stem: What most clearly distinguishes a political party from a special interest group?
options: A party is funded entirely by the Commonwealth government
A party has the authority to interpret the Constitution
A party seeks to win office by contesting elections
A party tries to influence policy without seeking office
questions.explanation: Political parties stand candidates at elections in order to win office and form government. Interest groups try to influence policy without seeking office themselves, which is the key difference between the two.

questions.stem: How does a social movement typically differ from a special interest group?
options: It is a government agency that gives ministers expert advice on a particular area of policy
It is a body that represents the business interests of the members of a single profession
It is a broad, loosely organised network of people seeking wide social or political change
It is a registered party that stands candidates at elections in order to form government
questions.explanation: Social movements are broad, often informal networks of people and groups united by a cause, such as environmental or civil rights movements. A body representing one profession's interests is a special interest group, which is usually more formally organised.

questions.stem: An association that represents the owners of pharmacies lobbies the government over the rules for selling medicines. It is best classified as:
options: a political party
a sectional interest group
a promotional interest group
a social movement
questions.explanation: A sectional (or protective) group represents the interests of a particular section of society, such as an occupation or industry, and its membership is limited to that section. A promotional group campaigns for a cause and is open to anyone who supports it.

questions.stem: An organisation campaigns for better treatment of farm animals and welcomes anyone who supports its aims as a member. It is best classified as:
options: an institution of government
a political party
a promotional interest group
a sectional interest group
questions.explanation: A promotional (or cause) group pursues a cause rather than the material interests of its own members, and membership is open to anyone who shares its goal. A sectional group represents the interests of a particular group, such as an industry or profession.

questions.stem: The High Court's main source of power in Australian politics is its authority to:
options: propose changes to the Constitution at referendums
veto bills before they are debated in parliament
decide whether laws are valid under the Constitution
dismiss a government that has lost public support
questions.explanation: Through judicial review, the High Court can declare a law invalid if it goes beyond the powers the Constitution gives, which makes it a powerful check on parliaments. It does not dismiss governments, and changes to the Constitution must start as bills in parliament.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth passes a law relying on one of its listed powers. The High Court rules that the law goes beyond that power and is invalid. What does this illustrate?
options: Popular sovereignty requires a referendum before the Court can make its ruling
The judiciary checks the legislature by enforcing the limits set by the Constitution
Parliamentary sovereignty means the Court's ruling is advisory and can be ignored
Responsible government allows the Court to dismiss the ministers responsible
questions.explanation: The High Court's ruling shows the separation of judicial power at work: an independent court holds parliament to the limits of its constitutional powers. The ruling is binding, not advisory, because Australian parliaments are bound by a written Constitution.

questions.stem: Describing the media as the 'fourth estate' refers to its role in:
options: conducting elections and counting the votes cast
advising the Governor-General on which judges to appoint to the courts
scrutinising those in power and informing the public
drafting legislation for debate in the parliament
questions.explanation: The 'fourth estate' describes the media's role as a watchdog that holds governments and other powerful actors to account by investigating and reporting on them. Conducting elections is the job of independent electoral commissions.

questions.stem: A newspaper runs a week of front-page stories on hospital waiting times, and the issue then rises in surveys of voters' main concerns. This best shows the media's power to:
options: decide the result of the next election in each marginal electorate
set the agenda by shaping which issues the public sees as important
make binding decisions about how health funding should be allocated
veto the government's health policies by refusing to report on them
questions.explanation: Agenda-setting is the media's capacity to influence which issues the public and politicians pay attention to, by choosing what to cover and how prominently. The media cannot make binding funding decisions, which belong to governments.

questions.stem: The political power of large corporations comes mainly from:
options: control of armed forces that can be used to enforce their interests
economic resources, such as investment, jobs and money for lobbying
constitutional authority to make laws for the regions they work in
the right of their executives to vote on bills in the parliament
questions.explanation: Corporations draw their power from economic resources: governments care about the jobs and investment they provide, and they can fund lobbying and campaigns. They have no constitutional authority to make laws.

questions.stem: A minister directs a government department to change how it delivers a program. The minister's power in this case comes mainly from:
options: military capacity
authority and office
leadership qualities
economic resources
questions.explanation: The minister can give the direction because of the authority attached to the ministerial office, which is accepted as legitimate. Leadership qualities can add to a minister's influence, but the power to direct a department comes from holding the office.

questions.stem: A community leader who holds no public office persuades thousands of people to join a campaign through skilled speaking and a strong personal reputation. This is power based mainly on:
options: authority and office
parliamentary sovereignty
military capacity
leadership qualities
questions.explanation: The leader has no office to draw on, so their influence comes from personal qualities such as persuasiveness and reputation. Authority and office would require holding a position, such as minister or member of parliament.

questions.stem: A proposed change to the Australian Constitution wins 54% of the national vote but a majority in only three states. What is the result?
options: It passes, provided both Houses of parliament approve it again after the vote
It fails, because a change to the Constitution needs two-thirds of the national vote
It fails, because it also needs a majority of voters in at least four of the six states
It passes, because a majority of voters across the nation is all that is required
questions.explanation: Section 128 requires a double majority: a majority of voters nationally and a majority of voters in a majority of states, which means at least four of the six. Winning only three states means the proposal fails despite its national majority.

questions.stem: In a referendum to change the Constitution, the votes of electors in the Australian Capital Territory and the Northern Territory count:
options: towards the national majority and towards a majority of states
towards neither majority, because territories have no say in referendums
towards a majority of states only, because territories are treated as states
towards the national majority but not towards a majority of states
questions.explanation: Territory electors vote in referendums and their votes are included in the national total. The second part of the double majority counts only the six states, so territory votes do not count towards it.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Australian states as political actors is most accurate?
options: They have no power to make laws on any matter listed among the Commonwealth's concurrent powers
They have power to make treaties with other countries on matters the Constitution leaves to them
They have power over residual matters such as policing, which the Constitution does not give the Commonwealth
They have power only over matters that the Commonwealth Parliament delegates to them by ordinary Act
questions.explanation: Matters not given to the Commonwealth, such as policing and most criminal law, remain with the states as residual powers. States can also legislate on concurrent matters, subject to section 109. Foreign affairs and treaty-making belong to the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: A citizen wants to give evidence to parliament about a proposed bill. The most direct formal way to do so is:
options: making a submission to a parliamentary committee inquiry
lodging an appeal against the bill in the High Court of Australia
writing to the Governor-General to ask for a veto
applying to the Australian Electoral Commission
questions.explanation: Parliamentary committees invite submissions from the public when they inquire into bills and issues, and may call people to give evidence at hearings. The High Court can rule only on laws in actual cases, not on bills that have not been passed.

questions.stem: Joining a political party gives an ordinary citizen access to power mainly because members can:
options: choose not to vote at federal elections
help choose candidates and shape the party's policies
vote on bills when the parliament is sitting
appoint the ministers in a newly elected government
questions.explanation: Party members can take part in choosing candidates (preselection) and in debating and setting party policy, which gives them a say inside an organisation that may form government. Only members of parliament vote on bills.

questions.stem: A social movement organises large protests and an online campaign, and the government later changes its policy. Which evidence would most strengthen a claim that the movement was politically significant?
options: Government statements and documents showing the policy changed because of the movement's pressure
The number of followers the movement's accounts gained on social media during the campaign
The fact that the movement's leaders were already well known before the campaign began
The fact that the movement published a clearly written statement of its aims and values
questions.explanation: Political significance is judged by impact, such as whether an actor changed the outcome or other actors' behaviour. Evidence linking the policy change to the movement's pressure shows that impact directly, whereas follower numbers show reach, which may or may not have affected the decision.

questions.stem: In VCE Politics, an actor's political perspective is best described as:
options: the resources it can draw on to influence an outcome, such as money or authority
the belief of other people that the actor has a legitimate right to exercise power
the position from which it sees an issue, shaped by its ideology, values and experiences
the goals it wants to achieve or protect in an issue, such as winning votes or profits
questions.explanation: A perspective is the lens through which an actor understands an issue and its interests, shaped by ideology, values, history and context. The goals an actor wants to achieve are its interests, which are related but distinct.

questions.stem: Which statement about political stability is consistent with the way it is understood in VCE Politics?
options: Stability exists only where actors have no competing interests on an issue
Stability can be achieved only through free and fair democratic elections
Stability is not always desirable, because it can protect an unjust status quo
Stability is always desirable, because any political change causes serious conflict
questions.explanation: Stability means the status quo is maintained, and that may preserve injustice, so change can be desirable and can itself bring stability. Competing interests exist in every political issue, so stability cannot depend on their absence.
